thread.title_full: Small Business Administration's new advocate promises aid for manufacturing, automation - NewsBreak

author: Rebecca Raney
title: Small Business Administration's new advocate promises aid for manufacturing, automation - NewsBreak
text: The United States’ Small Business Administration’s newest regional advocate for the Southeast hit the ground running Tuesday with a Red Tape Roundtable and several business tours in East Tennessee. Michael Vallante took over as regional advocate for the Southeast in early July. In a brief introductory email, Vallante described the SBA’s Office of Advocacy as “the watchdog for America’s small businesses on regulatory issues,” with his job being to “talk with businesses about the regulatory burdens they face, how it can be addressed and ensure their information gets back to decision-makers in Washington, D.C.” “The Office of Advocacy is specifically there in the SBA to find out from businesses the rules, the regulations, the pain points that they have that inhibit doing business,” said Vallante. “There is a fine line between success and failure for small businesses, and one little thing can make a huge difference. So, if someone in Washington sits in a cubicle and comes up with an idea which they think is good but actually does more harm than good, our job is to talk to the small businesses, find out what’s going on and bring that back up to Washington.” Under the guidance of Kelly Loeffler, SBA Administrator, the independent executive agency is responsible for supporting domestic small business owners and entrepreneurs lobbying for the passage or removal of certain regulations, connecting business owners with capital investment and loan opportunities and generally increasing the number of locally-owned businesses within the United States. Tuesday marked the start of Vallante’s on-the-ground operations. Flanked by Regional Administrator Tyler Teresa and District Director for Tennessee David Glasgow, Vallante marked his first official month on the job with the roundtable and some brief tours. “Today’s roundtable was an amazing first start. It took a little pulling and people were a little hesitant at first, but once they opened up, we heard some really critical stuff. One of the things I got from many different business owners was that it seems money doesn’t go as far as it used to. The economy’s just not there to support business as it was, and some of the regulations we’ve had in place for awhile now just don’t make sense now based on those economic challenges,” said Vallante. “We’ll take that with us to D.C. and work towards getting some relief for our business owners.” Goals As a cabinet-level agency, part of the SBA’s responsibilities are also to help fulfill domestic policy as established by the sitting president, which is why Vallante and other SBA officials visited a few local manufacturing and automation businesses Tuesday like Navus Automation Inc. Located on 2640 Westcott Blvd, Knoxville, Navus provides engineering and robotics-related automation services for clients as small as local home manufacturers, to ones as large as the Department of Defense itself. At just 25 total employees, general manager Curtis Brayman said the organization runs on some pretty tight margins, particularly in the post-pandemic landscape. Add to that the global uncertainty surrounding President Donald J Trump’s tariffs and calls to bring more manufacturing jobs to the states, Navus and companies like it are facing increased pressure to meet supply needs at-home under the same regulatory framework as they’ve operated in previous years. Vallante said that’s where he and the rest of the Office of Advocacy team come in. Their current work focuses on cutting back what Vallante described as “unnecessary” regulations and promoting “high-paying” American jobs and careers. Teresa added that although the SBA has previously done roundtables like these, Trump’s push to bring manufacturing back stateside has charged the department to hustle like never before. “With President Trump, if there’s one new federal regulation, he wants to get rid of ten others,” said Teresa. “Since this initiative just started in January, we’re going around, we’ve got a hotline set up, just trying to hear from local businesses about what they’re facing and how we can help.” Balance Between 26 and 39% of small businesses in Tennessee rely on, or intersect with, the tourism industry, according to an SBA state profile which documented more than 740,000 active small businesses. Since Maryville and Townsend are two of the state’s many aptly named “gateway” communities into the Great Smoky Mountains National Park and other acclaimed outdoor recreation opportunities, The Daily Times asked Vallante and Teresa how SBA planned to balance the needs of manufacturers with the needs of tourism-based businesses. “We work with departments like the Environmental Protection Agency, other regulatory agencies, to make sure these regulations won’t hurt Tennessee businesses in the tourism or hospitality areas, but also to make sure they aren’t crippling our manufacturers either,” said Teresa. “While we are here to talk about the red tape issues that are affecting manufacturing businesses here in Tennessee, and while a big goal of ours is to onshore more manufacturing jobs as President Trump has laid out, all Tennessee businesses can expect to be heard under Administrator Loeffler,” said Teresa. “Nothing is too big or too small for us to hear, especially since small businesses employ more people in the U.S. than large ones — not to say we don’t love our large businesses — but sometimes they don’t get heard as much as their larger peers with the corporate and lobbying capacity they have.” Visit SBA.gov for more information or to review the SBA’s online resources.
